Name: Leah
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. Can you tell me how you came to be working from home, and what it's like for you now?

Name: Glen
Transcript: Right. Well, I'm a claims handler, for an insurance firm. Motor claims, mostly, someone's gone into the back of someone at a roundabout. I've done it thirty-one years, in one form or another. And when the lockdown came we were all sent home, and when they asked us back, I asked if I could stay home. And they said yes, to my surprise. I'm sixty-three, I think they thought, he's not going to be here much longer anyway, let him get on with it. So it's been four years now. And it suits me. It suits me down to the ground.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What is it about it that suits you?

Name: Glen
Transcript: The quiet, mainly. I was on a floor with about eighty people, open plan, and it was noise all day. Phones, people shouting across. And there's a sort of, a performance to it, isn't there. Being one of the lads. Football on a Monday, who's had a few at the weekend. I was never very good at that. I'd do it, but it took it out of me. At home I just get on. I don't have to be anybody.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you take me through a normal working day, from when you get up?

Name: Glen
Transcript: I'm up at six, I always have been. Maureen, my wife, she's retired, she has a lie-in. I have my breakfast, I read the paper on the iPad. Then at quarter to eight I go upstairs to the box room. That was our daughter's room, she's long gone, she's in Bristol. I go up, I shut the door, and I'm at work. I start at eight. Claims, phone calls, the garage, the other side's insurers. I stop at twelve for lunch and I come down and Maureen and I have a sandwich together. Which is lovely. We never had that, all those years. Then back up at one, and I finish at half four, and I shut the laptop, and I say, that's you done. Out loud. To the room. Then I shut the door behind me.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You speak to the room.

Name: Glen
Transcript: I do. Maureen heard me once and thought I'd got someone up there. It's just, it's how I finish. Like turning the key in the shop. When I came down the stairs from the office, from the old office, I mean, I used to walk to the car park, twenty minutes in the car, radio on. That was my wind-down. And there isn't one now. So I say it to the room and I shut the door and that's my car park.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Where in your home do you work? What's that space like for you?

Name: Glen
Transcript: The box room. It's small. There's still a few of our daughter's things in the wardrobe. I've got the desk, a proper chair, a printer I never use. And it's, it's a work room now. That's important to me. I don't go in there at the weekend. If Maureen wants something out of the wardrobe at the weekend, she gets it. I don't go in. Because if I go in, I'll look at the laptop. And then I'll think about a claim. And then the weekend's gone.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What happens at the start and the end of your working day?

Name: Glen
Transcript: When I shut the door, and when I open it. Simple as that. It's the door. Some of the young ones at work, they're on their laptops in bed, on the settee. I don't know how they do it. You'd never stop. I need the door.

Name: Leah
Transcript: How has working from home changed things with the people you live with, or the people around you?

Name: Glen
Transcript: Well, Maureen, mostly. It's good. It's very good. But it took some getting used to, for both of us. She retired two years before me, before the pandemic, and she'd got her own routine. Her groups, her friends coming round. And suddenly I'm in the house. All day. And I think, at first, she'd come up and knock on the door. While you're here, love, can you have a look at the boiler. Since you're home, can you wait in for the man about the guttering. And I'd say, Maureen, I'm working. And she'd say, I know, I know. But she didn't, not really. It took us about a year to get it right.

Name: Leah
Transcript: How did you get it right?

Name: Glen
Transcript: We had a row. A proper one. About the guttering man, actually. And after that, I put a list on the fridge. My hours. Like a shop. And she laughed at it, but she stuck to it. And now I do the jobs after half four, and it's fine. Mind you, I think she'd say she's had to change more than me. She has her friends round on a Tuesday, and they whisper now. In their own house. Her house. I feel bad about that.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What's that like for you, hearing them whisper?

Name: Glen
Transcript: Odd. I'm up in the box room with my headset on, and I can hear them through the floor, going hush, hush, he's working. Like I'm the baby asleep upstairs. And I think, this was her house in the day, for two years. It was hers. And I've come home and taken a bit of it. She'd never say that. She'd say, don't be daft, Glen. But I know she misses having the place to herself. She said once she can't have the radio on in the kitchen any more. She can, I've told her she can. But she doesn't.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you tell me about a day working from home that has stayed with you?

Name: Glen
Transcript: It's not one day, it's more a thing that keeps happening. Our neighbour Brian, he's a lovely fella, but every time he sees me in the drive, he says, all right Glen, working hard or hardly working? Every single time. Four years. And I laugh, but it gets to me. Because he thinks I'm, you know, sat in my dressing gown. And I'm not. I'm in a shirt. I put a shirt on every day, collar, the lot. And I think that's partly for Brian, if I'm honest. And partly for me. So I know I'm at work. I've probably done more hours at home than I ever did in that office. I don't take a break in the afternoon like I used to. I don't have a natter at the kettle. I just work.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You said the shirt is partly for you.

Name: Glen
Transcript: It is. If I'm in a shirt, I'm at work. When I come down at half four, the first thing I do is go in the bedroom and take it off and put a jumper on. Maureen calls it my Val Doonican. She thinks that's very funny. But it's the same as the door, isn't it. You need something to tell you. Otherwise it's all just the house. And I'll tell you something else. I'm first on in the mornings. On the Teams. My little light's green at eight on the dot. I like them to see that. Silly, really, at my age. Thirty-one years and I still want the gaffer to see I'm in on time.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What do you think that's about, not taking the break?

Name: Glen
Transcript: I suppose I feel I've got to earn it. Being at home. Like it's a favour they've done me and I've got to prove it was worth it. Nobody's said that. My manager's never said that. But I'm sixty-three, and they could have me back in that office or out the door, and I'd rather they had no reason.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What, if anything, do you miss about working somewhere else? And what would you miss if you had to go back?

Name: Glen
Transcript: I miss very little, I'll be honest. I miss the car park, the drive home, like I said. That was mine. Radio Two and nobody wanting anything. And there was a lad, Darren, he left a few years ago, we used to go for a pint now and again. I miss that, a bit. But no, I don't miss it. And going back? I'd miss my sandwich with Maureen. Very much. And the money, you know, no petrol, no parking. I'd miss being able to just do my job, without the performance. That's what I'd miss.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Is there anything about working from home that we haven't touched on, that matters to you?

Name: Glen
Transcript: Only that sometimes I wonder if it's a rehearsal. For retiring. Because I'm in the house all day, and in two years I'll be in the house all day without the work. And I don't know what I'll do with the box room then. I'll probably still go up there at quarter to eight. Shut the door. Out of habit.
